title: Best No Matter What
question: A move that gives you the best outcome regardless of what the other player chooses has what name?
correctExplanation: Right. Dominance means your choice holds up across every possible reply, so no prediction of the opponent is needed.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a dominant strategy. It is defined by robustness to the other player's actions, not by highest payoff in one scenario. When a move wins under every reply, forecasting becomes unnecessary.
lessonContent:
Some choices do not depend on predicting others.
Dominance is about robustness across all replies.
Removing the need to forecast simplifies hard decisions.
Ask what happens under every opponent move, not just likely ones.
Share this: find one decision today that holds up regardless of what others do.

title: The Dominant Move
question: Two suspects are questioned separately in a one-shot prisoner's dilemma. Each does better personally by betraying, whatever the other does. What is the dominant move?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Betrayal dominates because it improves your own position under both possible choices by the other.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to defect. Each suspect reasons the same way, so both betray and both end worse than if they had stayed silent together. Individually rational choices can produce a collectively poor result.
lessonContent:
Individually rational moves can sum to collective loss.
Trust and cooperation are not guarantees; they are strategies.
Structure of incentives decides outcomes more than goodwill.
When both sides reason alike, symmetry predicts the result.
Share this: name one everyday situation where individual logic ruins a shared benefit.

title: Copy the Last Move
question: In repeated prisoner's dilemma tournaments, a simple rule won: cooperate first, then copy the opponent's previous move. What is this rule called?
correctExplanation: Right. Tit for tat stays nice, retaliates immediately, and forgives instantly — a combination that resists exploitation without locking into feuds.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is tit for tat. It opens with cooperation, then mirrors whatever came before. The power comes from being provokable and forgiving at the same time, which keeps long-run cooperation alive.
lessonContent:
Repetition changes the logic of defection.
Reciprocity rewards cooperation without being exploitable.
Forgiveness prevents feuds spinning out.
Simplicity can outperform clever schemes under noisy conditions.
Share this: try mirroring cooperation once today in a tense relationship.

title: Reasoning Backward
question: Which solution method begins at a game's final move and reasons step by step back to the opening, choosing optimally at each stage?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Backward induction starts from where choices run out and deduces which earlier moves survive rational play.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is backward induction. Anticipating how everyone will act later determines what you should do now. Reasoning forward alone misses that last moves constrain first ones.
lessonContent:
Terminal payoffs anchor the whole tree of choices.
Future rationality constrains present action.
Plan from the end to the start for sequential decisions.
Anticipating others' optimal responses changes your opening.
Share this: work one decision backward tonight starting at its outcome.

title: Centipede's First Node
question: In a long sequential game where moderate gains grow each round but a greedy grab ends play, backward induction tells the first player to do what at once?
acceptedAnswers: Cash out at the first move
correctExplanation: Right. Backward induction unpicks every future round until the first move is also a grab — the centipede game's unsettling conclusion.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to take immediately. Reason backward: nobody cooperates at the last round, which dooms the round before, and so on to the start. Experiments show people often cooperate anyway, revealing how much trust real behavior carries.
lessonContent:
Backward induction can produce counterintuitive first moves.
Each rational defection makes the prior round unstable.
Theory and observed trust often diverge sharply.
Knowing the formal answer does not dictate your best real choice.
Share this: notice tonight where your trust contradicts a pessimistic chain of reasoning.

title: The Cautious Prey
question: Two hunters can chase a big stag together or each catch a hare alone. Hunting the stag fails if either deserts, so safety favors the hare. Which choice is risk-dominant?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The hare pays modestly no matter what the partner does, making it the safer, risk-dominant option.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is the hare. The stag offers the biggest prize but collapses under mistrust, so the safer individual payoff dominates when confidence is low. Cooperation needs credible assurance, not just a better reward.
lessonContent:
Payoffs alone do not determine choices; confidence does.
Risk-dominant options protect against partner failure.
Big cooperative prizes demand trust or enforcement.
Assurance turns fragile cooperation into stable cooperation.
Share this: identify one group project that needs a trust mechanism before its big prize.

title: Matching Pennies Mix
question: In matching pennies, each player wants to match the other's coin — but only one can win each round. What kind of equilibrium does this game have?
correctExplanation: Right. Because any predictable choice gets punished, the equilibrium requires both players to randomize with equal probability.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a mixed equilibrium. No pure pair of choices is stable, since the loser always wants to switch. Equilibrium instead demands unpredictability — random play at specific odds.
lessonContent:
Some games have no stable pure choice pair.
Unpredictability can itself be the optimal strategy.
Mixed equilibria assign precise probabilities to each option.
Being predictable is a liability in zero-sum contests.
Share this: randomize one routine choice today to stay unreadable.

title: The Side Convention
question: Drivers must all pick a side of the road, and everyone benefits as long as all keep the same side. How many stable convention equilibria exist?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Left and right are equally stable once everyone coordinates on one; only consistency matters.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is two. Both sides work as conventions, and history decides which a country adopts. Coordination problems are solved by shared expectations, not by one objectively correct choice.
lessonContent:
Pure coordination has multiple equally good answers.
History and salience select among them.
Consistency, not correctness, creates the value.
Shared expectations substitute for communication.
Share this: name one convention you follow only because everyone else does.

title: The Salient Clue
question: Strangers told to meet in a city without contact often converge on the same obvious landmark. What is this salient shared solution point called?
correctExplanation: Right. A focal point works precisely because it stands out to everyone for the same reason, replacing communication with shared salience.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a focal point. Coordination without talking succeeds when one option is conspicuously obvious to all. Salience does the job that messages cannot.
lessonContent:
Shared salience can substitute for communication.
Prominent options attract mutual expectation.
Conventions and landmarks coordinate silently.
Predicting what others find obvious is a real skill.
Share this: guess tonight where a stranger would pick to meet in your city.

title: Tying Yourself Down
question: A sailor has himself tied to the mast so he cannot act on later temptation. What decision-theory device is he using?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Removing your own future options can strengthen your position — constraints become strategic assets.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a commitment. Limiting your own freedom now protects the plan your calmer self chose. Deadline apps, gym contracts, and locked savings accounts are modern descendants.
lessonContent:
Restricting future choices can improve outcomes.
Present-self and future-self often disagree.
Binding devices convert intentions into realities.
Commitment also strengthens credibility with others.
Share this: use one small binding device today to protect a good intention.

title: A Threat You'd Keep
question: A threat changes another player's behavior only if you would genuinely carry it out when the moment arrives. What is such a threat called?
correctExplanation: Right. Credibility is what separates a deterrent from an empty warning, and it usually requires changing your own incentives.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a credible threat. Bluffs fail once the other side can predict you would not follow through. Making the threat self-enforcing — or costly to abandon — restores its power.
lessonContent:
Threats only work when carrying them out is rational.
Bluffs unravel under forward reasoning.
Credibility often requires changing your own payoffs.
Reputation is how credibility accumulates over time.
Share this: test one warning you give tonight for whether you would really follow through.

title: Money Already Spent
question: Tickets are bought, the film looks terrible, and leaving feels like waste. What should a rational decider do with the money already spent?
correctExplanation: Exactly. Only future costs and benefits should guide the next choice; the paid ticket is gone either way.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to ignore it. The money is unrecoverable, so staying cannot bring it back or improve anything. Sunk costs should not influence a decision that is fully forward-looking.
lessonContent:
Past spending is irrelevant to future-optimal choices.
Continuing only to justify prior costs compounds losses.
Ask what the next hour offers, not what the last cost.
Walk away is a complete sentence.
Share this: leave one bad investment of time today without finishing it.

title: The Dollar Auction
question: In an auction where both the top two bidders pay and bids climb without limit, what pattern of behavior reliably takes over?
correctExplanation: Right. Once a bidder has sunk a large bid, quitting guarantees a loss while bidding raises the chance of recovery, so bids spiral upward.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is escalation. The rational-seeming reasoning to protect prior bids drives ruinous overbidding. Committing in advance to a limit is the standard defense.
lessonContent:
Traps can emerge from individually sensible steps.
Protecting sunk bids fuels runaway escalation.
Pre-set limits are the reliable countermeasure.
Exit rules must be made before the heat arrives.
Share this: set one hard limit in advance for an upcoming competitive decision.

title: The Winner's Burden
question: In an auction where the item's value is the same to everyone but unknown, what commonly happens to the person who wins?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The winner is usually the most optimistic estimator, so winning implies an estimate above the true value.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is that they overpay. Selection bias means the highest bidder is systematically the most overoptimistic. Rational bidders shade their estimates downward to counter this effect.
lessonContent:
Winning common-value auctions is itself evidence of overestimation.
Selection effects shape who wins, not just how much.
Shade estimates downward when many competitors bid.
Ask what winning tells you about your own estimate.
Share this: discount one shared-value estimate today by how many rivals have it.

title: Lemons and Collapse
question: When sellers know a used car's true quality but buyers cannot tell good from bad, what tends to happen to the market?
correctExplanation: Right. Buyers discount for uncertainty, good cars exit the market, and the average quality falls further — a downward spiral.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is that it unravels. Uncertainty drives prices toward the average, sellers of better cars withdraw, and quality drops in a self-reinforcing cycle. Guarantees, inspections, and warranties are institutional answers to this problem.
lessonContent:
Information asymmetry damages markets from within.
Average pricing punishes quality and rewards junk.
Institutions can restore trust where individuals cannot.
Warranties and inspections are economic technologies.
Share this: note one marketplace purchase today that leans on a guarantee.

title: Sorting the Careless
question: An insurer offers two policies, and careless drivers voluntarily pick the expensive one with lower coverage. What technique is the insurer using?
correctExplanation: Exactly. A menu of contracts lets people sort themselves by type, revealing private information through their own choices.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is screening. It works by making honesty attractive: each type prefers a different option. No interrogation is needed because the pricing reveals the hidden category.
lessonContent:
Menus can extract private information without interrogation.
Designing options so types self-select is the engine.
Incentives reveal what questions cannot.
Insurance, education, and pricing all rely on self-selection.
Share this: design one choice today that reveals a preference without asking.

title: The Costly Proof
question: A candidate earns an expensive qualification mostly to demonstrate determination to employers. What is this expensive proof called?
correctExplanation: Right. When the proof is costly enough, only genuinely able people find it worth acquiring, so it separates types.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is signalling. Unlike screening, the informed party acts first to reveal itself. Spending money or effort credibly conveys what cheap talk cannot.
lessonContent:
Costly acts can communicate what words cannot.
Signals work when imitators would find them too expensive.
Education, brands, and warranties all signal credibility.
Cheap talk earns no trust; expensive talk does.
Share this: identify one credential you trust because it is hard to fake.

title: Declining a Fair Bet
question: Offered a coin flip that pays $20 on heads and costs $10 on tails — perfectly fair odds — a person declines. What preference does this reveal?
correctExplanation: Exactly. The expected money is equal on both sides, so refusing implies that losing hurts more than winning pleases.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is risk aversion. It is not irrational — diminishing returns make each extra dollar worth less than the one lost. Choosing certainty over equal expected value is a preference, not an error.
lessonContent:
Equal expected value does not mean equal felt value.
Diminishing returns make losses loom larger.
Risk preferences are personal, not mathematical mistakes.
Insurance markets exist because losses hurt more.
Share this: identify one safe choice you make that a risk-neutral calculator would reject.

title: The Safest Worst Case
question: Which rule picks the option whose very worst outcome is the least bad — protecting against catastrophe first?
correctExplanation: Right. Maximin maximizes the minimum payoff, prioritizing survival over average return.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is maximin. It is deeply cautious: it ignores likelihoods and optimizes the floor. Great for avoiding ruin, poor at capturing upside when risks are safe.
lessonContent:
Worst-case rules protect the floor, not the ceiling.
Ignoring probabilities makes maximin very conservative.
Survival-first is right when ruin is irreversible.
Choose the rule to fit what you can afford to lose.
Share this: apply maximin once today to the riskiest item on your list.

title: The Least Regret
question: Which rule picks the option that minimizes the worst disappointment after seeing what would have been best?
correctExplanation: Exactly. It scores each option by how much worse it is than the best in hindsight, then minimizes that maximum gap.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is minimax regret. It is an emotional criterion as much as a financial one — designed for people who cannot bear knowing they chose badly. Different rules suit different people.
lessonContent:
Rules can optimize feelings instead of money.
Regret scores measure distance from the best hindsight option.
No rule is universally correct; criteria encode values.
Declare your decision rule before the stakes rise.
Share this: decide once today by least regret and notice how it feels.

title: The Coin's Stake
question: You stake $1 for a fair coin that pays $3 on heads and nothing on tails, so your net win is $2 on heads and a $1 loss on tails. What is the net expected gain?
correctExplanation: Right. Half of a $2 gain minus half of a $1 loss is a fifty-cent expected gain per play.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is fifty cents. Average the two outcomes: one half times two dollars minus one half times one dollar. Expectation describes long-run averages, not any single flip's result.
lessonContent:
Expected value averages outcomes weighted by probability.
Positive expectation does not guarantee individual wins.
Long-run averages require many repetitions.
Compute expectations before judging a wager lucky or unlucky.
Share this: calculate the expectation of one everyday gamble today.

title: Costly to Know
question: Learning enough to vote well costs far more time than one ballot can sway the result. What does decision theory say the rational move may be?
correctExplanation: Exactly. When the cost of information exceeds its expected effect, ignorance can be individually optimal.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is to stay uninformed. This is called rational ignorance: the incentive to learn collapses when one contribution barely matters. It explains much public apathy without appealing to laziness.
lessonContent:
Information has a cost and a marginal benefit.
Tiny individual influence weakens the incentive to learn.
Rational ignorance is a structural outcome, not stupidity.
Institutions can raise stakes to restore incentives.
Share this: notice one topic where the effort of learning exceeds your influence on it.

title: Blocking the Rival
question: Firms sometimes enter a market early specifically to deny a competitor the same opening. What strategic move is this?
correctExplanation: Right. The value is not just the market itself but keeping it out of others' hands — denying options can be worth more than seizing them.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is preemption. The firm runs ahead of the rival, not merely ahead of the trend. Blocking entry is a strategic motive distinct from ordinary profit seeking.
lessonContent:
Denying options to others is itself a strategy.
Timing can matter more than sheer efficiency.
First moves sometimes buy exclusivity, not just head start.
Weigh the value of blocking, not only the value of owning.
Share this: notice one race today where winning mattered mostly because a rival lost.

title: The Silent Giver
question: In a one-shot game where one player simply decides how to split a pot and the other must accept, what does a purely self-interested splitter give away?
correctExplanation: Exactly. With no consequences and no repeat play, self-interest keeps the whole pot.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is nothing. The dictator game isolates pure giving: no punishment, no reputation, no reciprocity. That real humans often give anyway is one of behavioral economics' most replicated results.
lessonContent:
Removing consequences strips away strategic motives.
What people give without reason reveals underlying preferences.
Real behavior often confounds pure self-interest models.
Fairness appears even when it costs the giver.
Share this: observe one unprompted generosity today and ask what incentive produced it.

title: No Better Alone
question: A set of strategies in which no player can improve by unilaterally changing is called what?
correctExplanation: Right. Unilateral deviation brings no benefit, so the configuration is self-enforcing even if everyone could do better by coordinating elsewhere.
incorrectExplanation: The answer is a Nash equilibrium. It means nobody gains from acting alone — not that the outcome is good. The prisoner's dilemma shows stable equilibria can be collectively terrible.
lessonContent:
Stability and desirability are separate properties.
Unilateral deviation tests define equilibrium.
Bad outcomes can be perfectly stable.
Escaping poor equilibria requires coordinated moves.
Share this: spot one stable-but-unhappy arrangement today and name what blocks change.
